Throughout our time in this course, we have completed five mini-projects which directly correlate to the note sections that they follow. The completion of these mini-projects helped solidify the theoretical ideas that related to the main themes of the course.  We can also see that they relate to each other, this provided support inf interconnecting the coursework sections we had completed or were going to complete in the upcoming weeks.

Reflection should include:

\* how each one ties into class content

 Beginning with mini-project 1, which heavily connected to the first section of notes on sampling distributions. In this project we simulated distributions for the minimum and maximum of various probability distributions. This connected both the ideas we saw in the first note packet, sampling distributions and order statistics. In the labs for the first section, we used statistical simulation to look at how sampling distributions could change. This mini-project was directly similar to this concept, just a bit more complex as we used more than one type of probability distribution. We can also see connections in all of the later sections, as we continuously saw the concept of a sampling distribution reappear, and we also continued to utilize statistical simulation in most of the labs and other mini-projects within the course. 

We then worked through Mini-project 2, which seemed to connect to all of the sections in the course, but less so to the section devoted to Bayesian statistics. This mini-project solidified our understanding of extremely important vocabulary, thus creating a foundation we could expand upon in later sections. A majority of these words had been introduced to us in our section on estimation (bias, consistent, variance, etc.) but there was also some which we had learned in section 1. As we worked through the class we continued to see a lot of these words (such as likelihood, parameter). Naturally, this mini-project connected to section 2 on estimation, where we derived a lot of estimators and estimates for different distributions and focused on their variance and bias. This project differed from the others because it didn't have any similar computations to the section that it followed, it was strictly completed to increase our knowledge of the vocabulary.

Mini-project 3 connected to the section based on confidence intervals, but it also had some overlap with section 5 on hypothesis testing. In this mini-project, we saw ways that the intervals would vary when given different parameters (proportion and sample size). This expanded on the notes and examples we worked through in section 3, where we learned how to calculate and interpret confidence intervals based on data, but the mini-project helped incorporate statistical simulation and understand how confidence intervals would react to unmet assumptions. This idea of breaking or meeting assumptions tied into the section on hypothesis testing, as we saw assumptions as being very important for test statistics which rely on the Central Limit Theorem. 

Mini-project 4 was unique, as it really only connected to the section 4 coursework. This section was different because it focused specifically on Bayesian statistics, and not frequentist statistics like all of the other sections. During this section, we focused on deriving posterior distributions from various prior distributions. These prior distributions were either non-informative or were created using a priori knowledge. Mini-project 4 directly relates to this idea as we used various informative and non-informative priors to display how they can alter the posterior distribution. Another way that this connected was through the creation of informative priors, which we could make based on knowledge from 'experts' and this was done in both our section coursework and the mini-project.


Our last mini-project was also quite unique, like the mini-project from section 2 it didn't have to do with computations. This mini-project was basically an analysis of the paper 'Moving to a world beyond p<0.05' by Wasserstein, Schirm, and Lazar. In this project we focused on understanding why using p-values and confidence intervals may not be the best practice, and how these values are seen as extremely reliable when in reality they are made based on data, not the truth. In the notes for section 5, we spend a lot of time learning how to calculate and interpret p-values, so this paper added a layer to our understanding of how we should be drawing conclusions and looking at results. Although this project didn't directly connect to the computations in the course, I thought it was a nice closing project and an enriching paper that helped us not just understand the metrics we have learned about, but the ways they are used in research. 

\* how they connect to eachother


\* biggest takeaways from the projects 

Each of these mini-projects had valuable lessons which applied to our coursework, but there were specific things that I took away from them. From the first mini-project, I learned more about the differences between some of the probability distributions we had focused on in STAT 325. Looking at the expected value and variances of the min/max showed me how the spread of each of these distributions can differ, and this project also really showed me how impactful statistical simulation is. 

The biggest takeaway that I took from the second mini-project is a little less theoretical. By writing this meaningful story I was able to work all of the vocab words together, and this helped strengthen my understanding of what they really mean (aside from a strict definition). 

The biggest takeaway that I took from the third mini-project relates to how broken assumptions will affect confidence intervals. When these assumptions are broken it can alter the width and coverage rate of the interval, which then affects the accuracy of your confidence interval interpretation. 

Through the fourth mini-project, I learned how influential the prior distribution is to the posterior distribution, and that by using different prior distributions you can create entirely different posterior distributions (which will then affect your conclusions). The idea I really took from this is the benefit to being able to adjust your distributions based on pre-existing knowledge (or with the addition of more data), which is unique to Bayesian stats. 

Lastly, the takeaway that I had from the fifth mini-project is that the reliance we have on p-values and confidence intervals is misguided and actually is limiting the scope of scientific research. From this paper, I learned the dangers of the strict division that significance contributes to research studies, and I also learned some opinions on how we should try to change this and approach results in a different way.
